prior_scientific_decisions.reason: For the assigned target Smaby, MacDonald, Ahearn, and Dube (2007), Fiske et al. (2019) explicitly state in the Introduction (p. 2) and Discussion (pp. 5-6, 8) that they systematically replicated the use of the multiple-schedule reinforcer assessment (MSA) procedure—reusing Smaby et al.'s rapid alternation between extinction and reinforcement components across two sequences alongside Cividini-Motta and Ahearn's (2013) star-pointing task and fixed component order—to evaluate the reinforcing efficacy of token-economy components in four new learners with ASD. In the Discussion (pp. 5-6), the comparison to Smaby et al. (2007) and Cividini-Motta and Ahearn (2013) is strictly methodological ('Similar to Smaby et al, the current study found the MSA to be a viable method to identify social consequences that function as reinforcers for children with ASD', and 'found the MSA to be suitable'), whereas substantive empirical comparisons of token-versus-primary reinforcement, tokens without backup, and delayed primary reinforcement are made to Fiske et al. (2015) and Leon et al. (2016). Under Codebook Step 3 Rules 2-3, agreement on a method's viability without comparing to a specific empirical finding of Smaby et al. (2007) is 'descriptive only'.

shipped_rows.outcome_quote: Token systems had reinforcing value similar to primary reinforcers for 2 of the 4 learners, but resulted in lower rates of responding than primary reinforcers for the other 2 learners. Differentiated responding across learners may warrant variation in clinical recommendations on the use of tokens. The results of this study support formal assessment of token system effectiveness, and the MSA procedure provides an efficient method by which to conduct such assessments.
